summary: Argentina grants visa-free entry of up to 90 days to citizens of the US, Canada, the UK, the EU, Australia, Japan and most of the Americas, charges no reciprocity fees any more, and offers an electronic travel authorization (AVE) to some visa-required nationals who hold a valid US visa.

conditionalWaivers.text: Chinese, Dominican and Indian ordinary-passport holders with a valid US visa of a similar category can enter Argentina without a consular visa or an AVE. Dominican and Indian citizens qualify for tourism only, for up to 90 days; Chinese citizens for tourism or business, for up to 30 days, and the Migraciones AVE page says a US green card also qualifies for them. The stay can be extended once for a similar period, and a change of immigration category is not allowed. The resolutions name only a US visa; anyone else needs a consular visa.

passportValidity.text: Argentina requires your passport to be valid for the duration of your stay; there is no formal 6-month rule, though airlines sometimes apply their own stricter checks.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Argentina entry requirements

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: Not an entry requirement. Argentina's Ministry of Health counts Misiones (including Iguazú Falls), Corrientes and Formosa, and parts of Jujuy, Salta and Chaco, as areas at risk of yellow fever circulation, and recommends vaccination at least 10 days before travel to areas with transmission.

source.name: Ministerio de Salud de la Nación — La vacuna contra la fiebre amarilla

conflict.name: WHO, International Travel and Health, Annex 1
conflict.states: risk of transmission only in Misiones and Corrientes provinces

travelInsurance.text: Since Decree 366/2025 (29 May 2025), every foreigner seeking admission must present a sworn declaration of the purpose of the visit and that they hold health insurance for their medical needs. Emergency care cannot be refused, but outside emergencies the national state's public hospitals treat non-resident foreigners only on presentation of health insurance or advance payment. No minimum cover is published.

source.name: Ley 25.871 de Migraciones (texto actualizado), arts. 8 and 34 as replaced by Decreto 366/2025
source.instrument: Ley 25.871, art. 34 (sworn declaration of health insurance on admission) and art. 8 (public health care for non-residents), as replaced by Decreto 366/2025, arts. 3 and 9 (B.O. 29/5/2025)

onwardTicket.text: Not a formal requirement, but airlines and immigration officers may ask for proof of return or onward travel and where you will stay.

source.name: Government of Canada — Travel advice and advisories: Argentina (entry and exit requirements)

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is set, but officers may ask about your means of support and travel plans when granting entry.

source.name: Government of Canada — Travel advice and advisories: Argentina (entry and exit requirements)

currencyLimits.text: Cash and monetary instruments worth USD 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared to customs on arrival. Taking USD 10,000 or more out of the country must be done by bank transfer, not in cash. For travelers under 16 the limit is USD 5,000.

source.name: ARCA — Viajeros: ingreso y egreso de valores

notes: Personal electronics such as a laptop and phone enter duty-free; keep receipts for expensive new items.
Strict controls apply to fresh food, plants and animal products, especially when crossing into Patagonia.

payments.text: Foreign cards are now widely accepted and charged at a market exchange rate, so paying by card is usually the simplest option; the old "blue dollar" cash premium has largely disappeared since the exchange-rate unification, though US dollar notes remain useful as backup. Inflation means peso prices change quickly.

safety.text: Argentina is one of the safer countries in Latin America. The main risk is petty theft — pickpocketing, bag-snatching and phone theft in Buenos Aires tourist areas such as La Boca, Retiro and on public transport. Avoid displaying phones and jewellery on the street.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Argentina travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: October to April (the southern spring, summer and fall) suits most itineraries — essential for Patagonia, pleasant in Buenos Aires and the wine regions; June–August is ski season in the Andes.

idp.text: Argentina is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

driving.text: Argentina is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1968 Vienna one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1949 Geneva version. A permit issued under the 1968 Vienna Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Argentina yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Geneva, 1949), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Geneva, 19 September 1949 (UNTS vol. 125, p. 3)

tips.text: Pay by foreign card where possible — international cards are settled at a market exchange rate since the FX unification, so the old need to carry stacks of US dollars for the "blue" rate has mostly gone. Keep some USD notes as backup and expect peso prices to move with inflation.

Ferries from Buenos Aires reach Colonia del Sacramento and Montevideo in Uruguay in 1–2 hours. Bring your passport, as you clear both countries' immigration at the terminal (Mercosur nationals can use ID cards).
Tap water is safe to drink in Buenos Aires and most Argentine cities; in remote rural areas ask locally or use bottled water.
Keep phones off café tables and be alert for distraction thefts ("mustard scam") in Buenos Aires tourist areas — petty theft, not violent crime, is the main visitor risk.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Argentina?
faq.answer: No. US citizens enter Argentina visa-free for tourism for up to 90 days. The old reciprocity fee was abolished years ago, so there is nothing to pay before travel.

faq.question: Can I extend my 90-day stay in Argentina?
faq.answer: Yes. You can request one 90-day extension (prórroga de permanencia) from the Dirección Nacional de Migraciones before your initial stay expires, online or at a Migraciones office.

faq.question: Do Chinese citizens need a visa for Argentina?
faq.answer: Chinese citizens need a consular tourist visa unless they hold a valid US visa, in which case they can enter without a visa or an AVE for tourism or business, for up to 30 days. Chinese citizens no longer apply for the AVE, and a Schengen visa does not qualify.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccine for Iguazú Falls?
faq.answer: It is not an entry requirement for Argentina, but the Ministry of Health counts Misiones (where Iguazú is), Corrientes, Formosa and parts of Jujuy, Salta and Chaco as yellow fever risk areas and recommends vaccination at least 10 days before visiting areas with transmission. Brazil-side visits make it even more advisable.

faq.question: Should I bring cash or use cards in Argentina?
faq.answer: Cards now work well: foreign Visa and Mastercard payments are converted at a market exchange rate, so card payments are usually as good as cash. Carry some US dollars or pesos as backup for small vendors and rural areas, and expect prices in pesos to rise frequently with inflation.
